date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Deut 29:1 states that the words of the covenant were commanded to be made with Israel in the land of Moab, "beside the covenant which he made with them in Horeb."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:1, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Deut 29:1 is the heading to chs. 29–30, not the close of the address in chs. 5–28.
claims.evidence: K&D on Deut 29:1 (against Schultz, Knobel, "and others"); Clarke dissents, reading it as the subscription to ch. 28 (see clm-deu-08-003). A scholarly judgment, not a textual fact.

claims.claim: In Hebrew texts Deut 29:1 is numbered 28:69, and 29:2–29 as 29:1–28.
claims.evidence: Clarke on Deut 29:1 ("distinguished as the 69th verse in some of the most correct copies of the Hebrew Bible"); BibleGateway note on Deut 29:1 ("In Hebrew texts 29:1 is numbered 28:69, and 29:2–29 is numbered 29:1–28").

claims.claim: Deut 29:2–9 rehearse Egypt, the signs and great miracles, forty years in the wilderness, and the defeat of Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:2–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "Yet the LORD hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day" (29:4) deplores Israel's insensibility after so many miracles; it does not excuse it.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:4 (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 29:2–4 (Moses "does not intend to excuse the previous want of susceptibility... but simply to explain the necessity for the repeated allusion," quoting Calvin); Clarke on 29:4 (the want of such a heart proves they "had grieved his Spirit, and abused the grace"). A commentary reading of the verse's force.

claims.claim: In the wilderness Israel's clothes and shoes did not wax old, and they ate no bread and drank no wine or strong drink, "that ye might know that I am the LORD your God" (29:5–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:5–6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out against Israel, were smitten, and their land was given to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh (29:7–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:7–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "Keep therefore the words of this covenant, and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do" (29:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The whole assembly stood before the LORD: captains/heads of tribes, elders, officers, all the men of Israel, little ones, wives, and the stranger in the camp, "from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water" (29:10–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:10–11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 29:10–11 (the stranger includes Egyptians from Ex 12:38 and Midianites with Hobab, Num 10:29).

claims.claim: The assembly entered into covenant and oath, that God might establish them as his people and be their God, as sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (29:12–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:12–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The covenant and oath were made not with those present only, but also "with him that is not here with us this day" (29:14–15) — i.e. with future generations.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:14–15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Clarke ("Him that is not here — all future generations of this people"); K&D (the covenant "was to embrace not only those who were living then, but their descendants also").

claims.claim: Israel had seen the abominations and idols of Egypt and of the nations they passed by — "wood and stone, silver and gold" (29:16–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:16–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D (*gillulim*, "lit., clods," cf. Lev 26:30).

claims.claim: The apostate is "a root that beareth gall and wormwood" (29:18); *rosh* is a plant of very bitter taste, not strictly a poisonous plant.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:18 (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 29:18 (*rosh* "is not, strictly speaking, a poisonous plant, although the word is used in Job 20:16 to denote the poison of serpents, because, in the estimation of a Hebrew, bitterness and poison were kindred terms"). The identification of the figure with idolatry's spreading corruption is the plain sense; the botanical gloss is K&D's.

claims.claim: The presumptuous hearer blesses himself, "I shall have peace, though I walk in the imagination of mine heart, to add drunkenness to thirst" (29:19); the sense of "to add drunkenness to thirst" is disputed.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:19 (BibleGateway KJV) (the speech is Established as text); K&D on 29:19 ("a proverbial expression, of which very different interpretations have been given," citing Rosenmüller and Knobel). The claim's assessment is Debated because the proverb's meaning, which the claim asserts as disputed, is not settled.

claims.claim: The LORD will not spare the presumptuous man; his anger and jealousy shall smoke against him, all the curses written in this book shall lie upon him, his name shall be blotted out from under heaven, and he shall be separated unto evil out of all the tribes of Israel (29:20–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:20–21, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: A coming generation and a stranger from a far land will see the land as brimstone, salt, and burning, like Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, and ask why; the answer will be that Israel forsook the covenant and served other gods, and the LORD rooted them out of their land "as it is this day" (29:22–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:22–28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 29:22–28 (Moses "foresees in the Spirit, and foretells... the devastation of the land by distant nations; as in Lev 26:31–32").

claims.claim: The locations of Admah and Zeboim (29:23) are not independently established.
claims.evidence: No source read in this session identifies a site for Admah or Zeboim. K&D identifies the four cities only generally as "the towns of the vale of Siddim (see at Gen 14:2)." No map pin may be given.

claims.claim: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law" (29:29).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:29, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Interpretive function is Traditional: JFB (said in answer to astonished inquiry whether Israel could ever deserve such punishments); Clarke (what God has revealed is essential; what he has not revealed "concern not man but God alone"); Matthew Henry (cf. Rom 11:33).

claims.claim: Deut 29 maps onto the ancient Near Eastern treaty form: historical prologue (29:2–9), parties covenanting (29:10–15), basic stipulations (29:16–19), curses (29:20–28), with 29:29–30:14 as repentance/restoration preaching and 30:15–20 as the covenantal decision.
claims.evidence: Constable on Deut 30, read in full (the mapping; citing Thompson p. 279, Miller p. 201, McCarthy *Treaty and Covenant* pp. 199–205, Baltzer *The Covenant Formulary* pp. 34–36 — **those scholars not read directly, second-hand via Constable**); Bible Odyssey, "Tablets and Treaties in the Ancient Near East," read in full (the four-part form). A scholarly comparison, not a proof of a date.

claims.claim: There is general consensus that Deut 29–30 (and 31:1–8) are not strictly part of the covenant document as such documents were ordinarily crafted, though the section serves a covenant function.
claims.evidence: Constable on Deut 30, read in full, reporting the consensus (citing Mayes pp. 358–59; Wenham; Merrill p. 375 — **none read directly, second-hand via Constable**). Capped at Probable for that reason.

claims.claim: When blessing and curse have come upon Israel and they call them to mind among the nations and return to the LORD with all heart and soul (30:1–2), God will act.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:1–2, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "The LORD thy God will turn thy captivity" (30:3) means to put an end to the distress (to turn the imprisonment), not "to bring back the prisoners."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:3 (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 30:3 (the Kal *shuv* "never has the force of the Hiphil"; cf. Job 42:10; Jer 30:8; Ezek 16:53; Ps 14:7; Ps 85:2; Ps 126:2, 4; Jer 29:14; Jer 30:18). A philological judgment.

claims.claim: God will gather Israel from all the nations, "even from the outmost parts of heaven," and fetch them (30:3–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:3–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The promised return to the land and multiplication "above thy fathers" (30:5) was not exhausted by the return from the Babylonian exile; its full scope is disputed.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:5 (BibleGateway KJV); JFB on 30:1–10 (not fulfilled by the Babylonian restoration; "not... of the Babylonish captivity that Moses was speaking"); Clarke on 30:4–6 (a more extensive captivity than Babylon is intended); K&D on 30:4–5 (fulfilment "does not take place all at once... commenced with small beginnings at the deliverance from the Babylonian exile"); Constable (repossession "to some extent" fulfilled by the Babylonian return).

claims.claim: "The LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live" (30:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Contrast with the command of Deut 10:16 ("Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart") — same phrase, different subject (see §8.3).

claims.claim: Deut 30:6 anticipates the new-covenant promises of a new heart: Jer 31:31–34 (law written on hearts) and Ezek 36:26–27 (new heart and new spirit).
claims.evidence: K&D on 30:6 (citing Ezek 11:19; Ezek 36:26; Jer 31:33); Constable on 30:1–10 ("Here Moses anticipated a new covenant... cf. Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:22–28"); Bible Odyssey, "Covenant in the Hebrew Bible," read in full (Jer 31:31–34 "proposes a new covenant based on the same observance of divine Torah"). The relationship is thematic/developmental, not quotation.

claims.claim: The LORD will put all these curses upon Israel's enemies and haters who persecuted them (30:7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Israel will return, obey all the commandments, and be made plenteous in every work, "for the LORD will again rejoice over thee for good, as he rejoiced over thy fathers," if they hearken and turn with all heart and soul (30:8–10); 30:9 repeats 28:11.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:8–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 30:9 (a repetition of Deut 28:11; "the fathers are not the patriarchs alone, but all the pious ancestors").

claims.claim: "This commandment... is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off" (30:11): *niphleth* means not too wonderful, i.e. not too hard to grasp or unintelligible.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:11 (BibleGateway KJV); Clarke on 30:11 ("not too wonderful or difficult... as the word *niphleth* implies"); K&D on 30:11–14 ("not too wonderful for thee, i.e., is not too hard to grasp, or unintelligible, vid., Deut 17:8"). A lexical judgment.

claims.claim: The word is not in heaven, nor beyond the sea, but "very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it" (30:12–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:12–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Rom 10:6–8 is a free adaptation of Deut 30:12–14, not a verbatim quotation: Paul keeps the "not in heaven / not beyond the sea / the word is nigh" skeleton, changes "beyond the sea" to "descend into the deep" (*abyssos*), and adds the glosses "(that is, to bring Christ down from above:)" and "(that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.)" and "that is, the word of faith, which we preach."
claims.evidence: KJV Rom 10:6–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV), compared word by word with Deut 30:12–14 (§3.4, §5.4); LXX Deut 30:13 ("go over... to the other side of the sea") does not account for "descend into the deep" (Vincent's Word Studies and Expositor's Greek Testament on Rom 10, via search excerpts — corroborating, not load-bearing); JFB, Clarke, and K&D on Deut 30:11–14 all agree Paul "applied" the passage.

claims.claim: The LXX of Deut 30:14 adds "and in thine hands to do it," which the MT/KJV lack; the LXX of 30:3 reads "the Lord shall heal thine iniquities" for "will turn thy captivity."
claims.evidence: Brenton's Septuagint Deut 30:3, 14 and LXX2012 Deut 30:11–14 (wording verified from three concordant online reproductions, including the Greek text: v. 14 *en tais chersin sou poiein auto*); Pulpit Commentary on Deut 30:3 notes the LXX rendering "and the Lord will heal thy sins" (via search excerpt). **Caveat:** the NETS critical edition was NOT read in this session (§12.4); the claim is about the LXX wording as reproduced, not about the NETS text.

claims.claim: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil" (30:15); obedience brings life and multiplication in the land, turning away to other gods brings perishing and short days (30:16–18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:15–18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 30:15–18 (summing up "the contents of the whole of this preaching of the law," as at Deut 11:26–27).

claims.claim: Moses calls heaven and earth to record, sets life and death, blessing and cursing before Israel, and says "therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live" (30:19) — heaven and earth standing in the witness role that gods filled in ancient treaties.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:19 (BibleGateway KJV) (the witnesses and the call are Established as text); the treaty-witness parallel is Probable: Constable on 30:11–20 ("Moses called the permanent, unchanging heaven and earth to witness... Those who made ancient Near Eastern treaties commonly called witnesses to attest them, as God did here"); K&D on 30:19 (heaven and earth as witnesses "as in Deut 4:26").

claims.claim: To love the LORD, obey his voice, and cleave unto him is "thy life, and the length of thy days," that Israel may dwell in the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (30:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 30:20, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); K&D on 30:20 ("for that (namely, to love the Lord) is thy life... vid., Deut 4:40").

claims.claim: The text's literary horizon is a complete future arc spoken from Moab: blessing and curse will come, Israel will be scattered among the nations, will return, will be gathered from the outmost parts of heaven, and will be restored to the land with circumcised hearts.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:22–28; 30:1–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). This is what the text presents; it is not a dating claim (see clm-deu-08-037).

claims.claim: The composition date of Deut 29–30, and of 30:1–10 in particular, cannot be inferred from the exile language alone; whether the passage is pre-exilic prophecy, exilic, or post-exilic composition is debated.
claims.evidence: No modern critical argument on the date was read directly in this session. Second-hand positions reported via Coffman (search excerpts only — **not read directly**): Wright, *Interpreter's Bible* (1954), pp. 508–509 ("No proof can be adduced that it could not have been written in the seventh as well as in the sixth century"); von Rad, *Deuteronomy* (1966), p. 183; Phillips, *Deuteronomy* (1973), p. 198; Coffman's own position is Mosaic prophecy, c. 1400 BCE. K&D (read in full) take a multi-era fulfilment view that does not settle a composition date. Capped at Debated; a library-access task should read one critical argument in full before publication gives the dating question prominence.

claims.claim: The Babylonian exile (fall of Jerusalem, 586 BCE) is the historical exile that later readers and the prophets associate with Deut 30's return language; the return from Babylon is a partial, not exhaustive, fulfilment of 30:1–10.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "Covenant in the Hebrew Bible," read in full ("the dynasty of David ruled for only four centuries, until the Babylonian exile in 586 B.C.E. (2Kgs 25)"); JFB and Clarke on 30:1–10 (the Babylonian return did not match the passage's terms); K&D on 30:6 (fulfilment "commenced with small beginnings at the deliverance from the Babylonian exile"). The 586 date is Established as history; the association with Deut 30 is interpretive, hence Probable.

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence for the Moab covenant ceremony of Deut 29–30.
claims.evidence: §6.2 — the negative fact, stated as such. No inscription, sanctuary, or artefact read in this session can be tied to Deut 29–30.

claims.claim: The narrated setting is the plains of Moab east of the Jordan opposite Jericho; the exact ground of the ceremony is not established and no map pin may claim a verified event location.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 29:1, 7 (BibleGateway KJV) ("this place"); Num 22:1; Deut 34:8 (plains of Moab) as the regional setting. The region is what the text states; the exact ground is Unknown (no source read identifies one). Assessed Traditional for the regional setting, with the exact ground explicitly Unknown in the evidence.

claims.claim: The Moab covenant is a renewal — a renewed declaration of, and fresh obligation to keep, the Horeb covenant — not a second distinct covenant; no new sacrifice or blood rite is recorded in Deut 29–30.
claims.evidence: K&D, introduction to Deut 29–30 (read in full); JFB on 29:1 ("It was substantially the same; but it was renewed now, in different circumstances"); Clarke on 29:1 (an "additional institution to the ten words given on Horeb"). The absence of a sacrifice/blood rite in the text is Established as a textual observation; the "renewal, not second covenant" reading is Probable.

claims.claim: "Palestinian Covenant" is a later theological label for Deut 30:1–10, not a distinct covenant in the text; the verses elaborate the land promises already made to Abraham.
claims.evidence: Constable on 30:1–10, read in full (the label's use by Chafer, *Systematic Theology* 4:317–23; Pentecost; Scofield; and the note that "these verses do not constitute a distinctively different covenant. They simply elaborate on the land promises made earlier to Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 12:7; et al.)"; Miller p. 200 is cited for the contrary view that chs. 29–30 are a distinct covenant — **Miller not read directly**).

connections.note: The Horeb covenant beside which the Moab covenant stands; "a peculiar treasure... a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation."
The Horeb covenant "not with our fathers only, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day."
The signs and great miracles in Egypt that the retrospect recalls; broad background range, one continuous passage.
Paul's composite quotation: "God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear;) unto this day" — Deut 29:4 + Isa 29:10.
The wilderness provision: manna, and raiment not waxing old.
The battles with Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan.
Moses' fuller account of the same Transjordan conquest (category 1's range; cited here as the parallel account, not re-argued).
The next covenant renewal: Shechem, the same pattern of assembly, recital, and oath.
The patriarchal oath the Moab covenant fulfils: "to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee."
"Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled" — the root of 29:18. K&D and JFB both note the link.
"An evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God" — Clarke cites Heb 3:12 on 29:18–19.
"All the curses that are written in this book" — the curses of ch. 28 (category 7).
Desolation, exile, and the land enjoying its sabbaths; K&D cites Lev 26:31–32 on 29:22.
The overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, the comparison for the devastated land.
"O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments" — JFB and Matthew Henry both link 29:29 with Paul's close of Rom 11.

Solomon's prayer: if they "bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent... and pray unto thee toward their land." The same pattern (captivity → remembrance → return) before the exile.
Confession in the land of their enemies, uncircumcised hearts humbled, and God remembering the covenant of their ancestors (K&D cites Lev 26:40 on 30:1).

Nehemiah's prayer quotes the gathering promise ("If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations... if ye turn unto me... I will gather them thence"). JFB notes Neh 1:8–9 sanctions reading 30:1–10 as pointing to several similar eras.
"I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places whither I have driven you" — the gathering promise taken up in the exilic letter.
The command ("Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart") beside the promise ("the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart"). Same phrase, different subject.
"Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem."
The new covenant: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts" (K&D cites Jer 31:33 on 30:6; Constable cites Jer 31:31–34).
"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you... I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (K&D cites Ezek 36:26 on 30:6).
"Circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter" — Clarke cites Rom 2:29 on 30:6.
"Circumcised with the circumcision made without hands" — Clarke cites Col 2:11–12 on 30:6.

Paul's free adaptation (not verbatim quotation) of Deut 30:12–14 — a word-by-word comparison shows the adaptation: Paul keeps the "not in heaven / not beyond the sea / the word is nigh" skeleton, changes "beyond the sea" to "descend into the deep," and adds glosses.
"Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse" — the same choice, earlier in the book (K&D cites Deut 11:26–27 on 30:15).
Heaven and earth called to witness against Israel (K&D cites Deut 4:26 on 30:19).
"It is not a vain thing for you; because it is your life" — "he is thy life, and the length of thy days" (K&D cites Deut 32:47 on 30:15).
